label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**Why I'm Keeping the Busing Project (or: a long reply to a short text)**

Jess texted me last night: "It's one assignment. Don't torch your job over it." About half the group chat agreed, and a couple of you sent the grimacing emoji, which I've decided to read as support. I started typing back and realized I was about to send fifteen messages, each one a little more defensive than the last. So I'm writing it here instead, once, the long way.

This is mostly for Jess. Everyone else is welcome to read over her shoulder.

**What happened**

For anyone who missed it: every fall my juniors in US History II (two sections) do an oral history project on busing and desegregation in Boston, 1974 to 1976. They find someone in their family or neighborhood who was around then, record a ten-minute interview, and write a two-page reflection. I've done it at Cobb Street for four years. Until this month, nobody had ever complained.

A parent emailed Dr. Halvorsen and cc'd someone on the school committee. She said the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents." Halvorsen called me in and, very politely, suggested I might want to quietly let it go this year. Nothing official. Just a suggestion, the way principals make suggestions.

There's a meeting with Halvorsen and the parent next Thursday, the 19th, at 3:15. I'm going to tell them I'm keeping it.

**Jess, you're not wrong**

I want to say this first so it doesn't get buried. You're not wrong that I could get burned. I've had tenure since 2021, so I'm not going to get fired over a reflection paper. But Halvorsen still decides my schedule, and she decides who teaches AP. There are a lot of quiet ways to make a teacher's life worse without anyone ever writing a memo. You've worked in HR for years now. You know how this goes better than I do.

And honestly, I'm a little scared. I'd love to tell you I'm calm and principled about it, but I've rehearsed the Thursday meeting in the shower about nine times and lost the argument in at least four of them. So this isn't me being brave. It's me deciding that I'd rather be scared and keep it than be comfortable and drop it.

**Why it matters to me**

This is the history of the city these kids live in. Some of them ride past South Boston High on the way to practice. Their grandparents were on the buses, or driving them, or standing on the sidewalk, or keeping their kids home, or doing none of that and just watching it on Channel 5 and saying nothing at dinner. Our textbook gives the whole thing one paragraph. One paragraph, for something that shaped which neighborhoods people live in, where they send their kids, and who they still won't talk to at a wake.

If I don't teach it, the kids don't get some neutral, wound-free version of history instead. They get the version they absorb at home, which is usually a few sentences and a change of subject.

Two students make my case better than I can.

In 2023 a kid I'll call D. interviewed his grandmother. It turned out she'd driven a school bus in Southie in '74. She had never told anyone in the family. Not her kids, not her grandkids, nobody. D. asked if he could play part of the recording for the class, and he played about forty seconds of her describing one morning on her route. When it ended, nobody said anything for close to a minute. Thirty juniors, total silence, on a Tuesday. I've been teaching fourteen years and I can count on one hand the times a room has been that quiet for the right reasons.

Last year a girl found out during her interview that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was really upset. She stayed after class, and then stayed after again a few days later, and we just talked it through. Mostly she talked and I listened. Then she turned in her reflection, and it was the best thing I read all year. She didn't let her uncle off the hook, and she didn't turn him into a cartoon either. She wrote about loving someone who did something ugly, and about what it means that he's sorry now, if he's sorry. She's seventeen. Plenty of adults never get there.

So when the email says the project "reopens wounds," my honest answer is that the wounds were never closed. They just got quiet. That girl's family had been carrying her uncle's story the whole time. She just hadn't known.

**But the parent has a point**

I mean this. I'm not walking into Thursday looking for a fight.

The "pressure" part landed with me. When I set the assignment up as "interview someone in your family," I was thinking about the kids like D., where it opens something up. I wasn't thinking hard enough about the kid whose family situation makes that conversation impossible, or unsafe, or just too much right now. For that kid, the assignment can feel like being told to put their grandparent on trial for a grade, and that's not fair to them.

Here's my line. I think the students who are most uncomfortable with this history are often the ones who most need to sit with it. But I don't get to force anyone. Those two things are both true, and the assignment has to make room for both.

So my plan for Thursday is to keep the project and add an alternate route. No student will *have* to interview family. They can interview a librarian or an archivist instead. Plenty of people in this city have studied this period and are happy to talk about it. Or they can work from recorded interviews from past years, with permission from the students and families who made them. Same reflection, same rigor, no kid stuck in a conversation they're not ready for at home.

I'm going to tell the parent she was right about that, because she was. I'm hoping that if I start there, we can talk about the rest like people instead of like a complaint and a response.

**What I'm actually asking**

Jess, I'm not asking you to agree with me. You might still think I'm being stubborn about a reflection paper, and you might be right. You've been the more practical one since we were both student teaching in 2012, sharing a copier and pretending we knew what we were doing. You were usually right then, too.

I just wanted you to know why. Not "because I'm stubborn" (though, sure, a little). Because I've watched this assignment do something for kids that almost nothing else I teach does, and because I think the version of this school where we quietly drop the hard stuff whenever someone emails the committee is a worse school. I'd rather walk into that meeting with a better assignment than walk out with no assignment.

If it goes badly, you're allowed to say "I told you so." Once. Then you have to buy the drinks.

I'll text you Thursday after the meeting, probably around 4:30, probably from my car in the parking lot, probably in all caps either way.

Thanks for worrying about me. I mean that. It's one of my favorite things about you, even when it shows up as a text telling me I'm about to do something dumb.
